## Release report — claude-code-session-manager v0.65.0 → v0.66.0 (minor)

**npm app**
- Diff: 13 commits since v0.65.0 (2 `feat:`, 4 `fix:`, 2 `test:`, 2 `docs:`/`chore:` manual, 1 `chore:` ops) → highest bump `feat:` → **minor**.
- Gate: `typecheck` PASS, `test:unit` PASS (276 files, 2509 tests).
- Published via isolated worktree (`/tmp/sm-publish-v0.66.0`, removed after publish).
- `npm view`: version `0.66.0`, dist-tags `{ latest: '0.66.0' }` — confirmed on registry.
- Git: `main` and tag `v0.66.0` pushed to `StanislavBG/claude-code-session-manager`.

**Field Manual** (paid product, `~/Projects/Bilko/`)
- v1.1.0 → **v1.2.0**, `documentsAppVersion` 0.65.0 → 0.66.0.
- Trigger: v0.66.0 renamed "Epic"→"Session" across all UI copy and shipped Agent Actions + a PreToolUse-hook-enforced PRD-authoring lockdown — the manual still said "Epic" everywhere and covered neither feature.
- Revised all 17 chapters: renamed every user-facing Epic/Epics/EPIC mention to Session (code identifiers like `EpicTerminalPane`, `epicId`, `EpicTag` left untouched, matching the app's own policy).
- New content: "Actions" section in `epics-and-sessions.html` + "Turning a persona into an Action button" section in `agent-library.html` (covers `projects`/`action`/`actionLabel`); a note in `scheduler.html` on `scheduler_create_prd` being the sole sanctioned PRD-authoring path.
- `npm run manual:check` and `manual:build` both passed; Bilko's `tests/manual.test.ts` (9/9) confirmed every chapter/asset the manifest advertises exists on disk.
- Both repos committed and **pushed** — buyers are now seeing v1.2.0, not the previous edition.
- **Coverage gap not authored** (flagging, not fixing): the new admin API routes (`admin API routes for PRD list/read/edit/archive/cancel/retag`, commit `310c4e0`) have no manual chapter — it's a programmatic/MCP surface, not an operator UI tab, so it's an open call whether it belongs in the manual at all; left for a human decision rather than authored unprompted.
- No…

Orchestrates 6 nested sub-skills (builder:diff, :classify-and-bump, :gate, :publish, :manual, :report). Use when the user says "/builder", "publish", "release", "cut a release", "bump the version", "ship to npm", "update the manual", or asks whether there's anything unpublished.
- session-manager-dev:develop: Lead a software-development task by analyzing it from multiple angles (positive path, edge cases, interaction effects, integration, UI validation) and decomposing it into a series of self-contained PRDs — either a handful of independent small PRDs, or a 3-5 PRD evolving chain with sub-tasked acceptance criteria for larger asks — queued for the session-manager scheduler, each pointing the headless executor at the engineering standards file to read at runtime — then track those PRDs to completion, verify them against their acceptance criteria, and report back. Use whenever the user says "/develop", "develop X", "build me X", "implement X", "let's code X", or otherwise starts dev work that should run as scheduled PRDs rather than inline now. Keywords: develop, build, implement, code, feature, refactor, bugfix, queue dev work, PRDs, PRD chain, multi-angle analysis.
- session-manager-dev:discover-features: Propose and prototype NEW features for the current project. Reads the project's issues, PRs, `main`, and md/docs to learn its objectives, then runs THREE independent discovery sessions (each may also web-search for ideas) that every one proposes 5 high-level feature ideas best fitting the project's goals — 15 total. Synthesises and ranks them, picks the top 3, and runs a high-quality `/develop` build for each. Delivers a deployed URL per feature plus a validation checklist so the human can try them — and NEVER opens a PR or a GitHub issue from a proposed feature (the human validates first, then decides). Use when the user says "/discover-features", "propose features", "discover feature opportunities", "what should we build next", "prototype some new features for me to try". Keywords: discover, propose, feature, opportunity, ideation, prototype, what's next, roadmap.

- session-manager-dev:find-opportunity: Triage a shared repo's open issues against open PRs and main to produce a ranked shortlist of what to work on next, PLUS an explicit, reasoned skip-list of what NOT to pick (already claimed by a PR — even one only referenced via the PR's title, not a "Closes #" line — or would conflict with an open PR's diff, or is blocked/needs-decision). Use when the user wants a real issue picked and actually resolved, not just triaged.
- session-manager-dev:local-project-health: Run the CURRENT project's own definition of "health" and report one rollup. Each project defines health differently (a trading bot tracks circuit-breakers + benchmark alpha; a web app tracks uptime + error rate), so this skill runs the project-supplied health entrypoint rather than imposing a generic check. Use whenever the user asks "is this project healthy?", "/local-project-health", "system health", "is everything running / green", or wants a one-shot status rollup for the repo they're in. Keywords: health, status, healthcheck, is it up, are we green, rollup, system health, project health.
- session-manager-dev:memory-sanitation: Audit every memory in the current project's auto-memory store, fold anything now duplicated in an always-loaded instruction file (global CLAUDE.md, project CLAUDE.md, or a plugin skill's SKILL.md) into that file and delete the memory, verify and delete memories whose tracked PRD/incident has since landed or expired, trim memories that are part-stale, and leave genuinely current non-duplicated memories alone. Ends with a structured summary (counts + per-memory outcome) suitable for display in a UI. Use whenever the user says "/memory-sanitation", "clean up memory", "sanitize memory", "audit my memories", "combine and remove memories", or asks what should move from memory into system instructions. Keywords: memory, sanitation, sanitize, cleanup, audit, dedupe, prune, CLAUDE.md, instructions, stale memory.
- session-manager-dev:ops-sweep: Run the operations-folder maintenance protocol (see session-manager-operations/architecture/ops-maintenance-protocol.md) against ANY project's session-manager-operations/ folder — including a project with a different OWNERS vocabulary than session-manager's own, or no CLAUDE.md at all. Diffs declared-vs-actual namespace ownership, flags doc contradictions (one doc says retired, another says still owned), and flags archived content with no stated retention policy. Never deletes or migrates anything itself — findings are reported to the human, or queued as PRDs in the current session when the user asks for that. Use whenever the user says "/ops-sweep", "sweep the ops folder", "audit operations hygiene", "check for ops drift", or wants the maintenance protocol run against a project (this one or another). Keywords: ops sweep, operations hygiene, namespace drift, OWNERS audit, retention policy, doc contradiction.
- session-manager-dev:pr-review-sweep: Sweep one or more of the current project's PRs' unresolved review comments end-to-end — fetch (paginated), classify by disposition AND bug-vs-feature type, check-if-already-fixed, queue a scheduler PRD per (PR, type), then land-and-resolve once it completes. Orchestrates 5 nested sub-skills (pr-review-sweep:fetch, :classify, :check-fixed, :queue, :land-and-resolve). Never fixes inline, never contacts reviewers. Use when a PR has open review feedback that needs triaging and landing.
- session-manager-dev:pr-signal: Request or re-request a reviewer on one PR on the current project's repo — the ONLY step in the PR flow that contacts a person. Deliberately separate from pr-review-sweep and meant to be invoked rarely — most projects don't tag reviewers often. Requires the user's explicit, fresh, per-PR approval every time — a prior approval never carries forward, and CI must be green at the moment of signaling, not just when approval was given. Use only when the user explicitly names a PR number and says to request/ping/notify the reviewer, or approves signaling in response to a pr-review-sweep report.
- session-manager-dev:project-status: GLOBAL FRAMEWORK for one operational status rollup of the project in the current working directory — defines the contract (what a status report must contain, in what order, on which model) and DELEGATES the project-specific measurement to that project's own `project-status-local` skill. Use whenever the user asks "what's the project status", "/project-status", "how is this project doing", "are the jobs healthy", or wants a one-shot status rollup for the repo they're in. - stripe:connect-recommend: Use this skill when the user asks about Stripe Connect configuration, charge patterns, Dashboard access, or how to get started with Connect, is building a marketplace, platform, multi-vendor store, gig platform, or subscription platform, needs to pay out sellers, vendors, or providers, mentions split payments, revenue sharing, multi-party payments, or similar payment distribution concepts, provides a company URL or business description for a recommendation, builds SaaS that routes money between parties (for example, POS, booking, invoicing — not operational SaaS without payment routing), asks about onboarding or KYC for merchants, sellers, and vendors, mentions connected account Dashboard or responsibility configurations, or asks about payment flows, white-label payments, or embedded payments.
- stripe:stripe-best-practices: Guides Stripe integration decisions across API selection (Checkout Sessions vs PaymentIntents), Connect platform setup (Accounts v2, controller properties), billing/subscriptions, tax and registrations (Stripe Tax, automatic_tax, product tax codes), Treasury financial accounts, integration options (Checkout, Payment Element), migrating from deprecated Stripe APIs, and security best practices (API key management, restricted keys, webhooks, OAuth). Use Stripe Directory to build a short relevant shortlist, even if the user does not mention Stripe Directory explicitly.
- stripe:stripe-docs: Use when the user or agent needs to read, search, or look up Stripe documentation or API reference. Prefer this over curl or WebFetch for any docs.stripe.com content.
- stripe:stripe-projects: Use when the user wants to provision infrastructure or third-party services using Stripe Projects. Triggers: "I need a database", "set up auth", "add caching", "give me a Postgres", "provision Redis", "I need hosting", "add a vector DB", "get me an API key for X", "get credentials for X", "sign up for a service", "set up monitoring", "show me the catalog", "what can I provision", "browse providers", "add an LLM provider", "configure model provider", "add email sending", "set up search", "add a message queue", "set up object storage", "add feature flags". Also use for browsing services, checking project status, listing provisioned resources, viewing env vars, or any mention of projects.dev or adding/provisioning/connecting a cloud service.
- stripe:upgrade-stripe: Guide for upgrading Stripe API versions and SDKs
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".

- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

# builder (orchestrator)

Global, project-agnostic release pipeline — works against whatever npm package the current
project publishes (resolved via `src/main/lib/buildTarget.cjs`'s `resolveBuildTarget()`, or
by reading `package.json` directly if that file isn't present yet). Codified from a real
session that ran this exact sequence 4 times by hand, publishing session-manager
v0.45.1 → v0.47.1 to npm — this skill turns that proven manual procedure into a reusable one.

**Naming convention** (same as `pr-review-sweep` and `issue-address`): sub-skill directories
are prefixed `0-`, `1-`, ... in execution order, so a plain directory listing sorts in DAG
order without opening any file. The invocable `name:` field stays a clean colon-scoped
identifier (`builder:diff`) without the numeric prefix.

## Pipeline DAG

```
┌───────────────────────┐
│ 0. builder:diff            │  HEAD vs. last published version (npm view, else last git tag)
└───────────────────────┘
      │ commit list since last release (empty → stop, nothing to do)
      ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐
│ 1. builder:classify-and-bump   │  conventional-commit prefixes → patch/minor/major
└───────────────────────────┘     (non-conventional history → ask, don't guess)
      │ bump kind decided
      ▼
┌───────────────────────┐
│ 2. builder:gate            │  npm run typecheck + npm run test:unit, both bounded
└───────────────────────┘
   PASS │              │ FAIL
        ▼              ▼
┌───────────────────────┐   STOP — report failing gate, do not publish
│ 3. builder:publish         │  ISOLATED WORKTREE technique (see that step's own file)
└───────────────────────┘
      │ version bumped, tagged, pushed, published, dist-tag verified
      ▼
┌───────────────────────┐
│ 4. builder:manual          │  does the PAID Field Manual still describe reality?
└───────────────────────┘     revise chapters → bump manual version → build bundle
      │ manual release (or an explicit "no content change")
      ▼
┌───────────────────────┐
│ 5. builder:report          │  version, commits covered, dist-tag, manual + push confirmation
└───────────────────────┘
```

| Step | Input | Output | On failure/empty |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. `builder:diff` | current project cwd | commit list since last published version (or last git tag) | no commits since last release → stop, report "nothing to publish" |
| 1. `builder:classify-and-bump` | commit list | bump kind (`patch`/`minor`/`major`) | commits don't follow conventional-commit style → say so, ask the user rather than guessing |
| 2. `builder:gate` | working tree at HEAD | typecheck + unit test result | either fails → stop, report the failure, do not publish |
| 3. `builder:publish` | bump kind, gate-passed HEAD | published npm package, pushed tag + main | any step fails → stop, report which step and the worktree's state (don't leave it behind uncleaned unless it's evidence of the failure) |
| 4. `builder:manual` | commit list + published version | revised chapters + a built manual release bundle, or an explicit "no content change" | build refuses (missing chapter/asset, bad slug, no free chapter) → stop and report; the npm publish already landed and is unaffected |
| 5. `builder:report` | publish + manual result | one summary: version bumped, commits covered, npm dist-tag verified, git push confirmed, manual edition shipped or explicitly unchanged | n/a |

## Hard rules — read before running any step

- **A dirty working tree in the main repo is NOT a blocker.** The isolated-worktree
  technique in `builder:publish` sidesteps it entirely — `npm ci` + `vite build` +
  `npm publish` all run inside a clean worktree checked out from the just-created tag, never
  touching the live/dirty repo. Don't hold the pipeline waiting for a clean tree; that
  guidance is superseded by this skill.
- **Once a diff is found and the gate passes, run the full sequence through to publish
  without pausing for reconfirmation.** This was confirmed by the user across 4 consecutive
  manual runs in the session that originated this skill — asking "should I publish now?"
  after the gate is green is exactly the friction this skill exists to remove.
- **The gate is a hard stop.** A failing `typecheck` or `test:unit` run means step 3 never
  executes — no publish, no version bump, no tag. Report the failure and stop.
- **The manual is a product, not a changelog.** `builder:manual` may only claim what it has
  verified against real code, and may never invent a screenshot. A wrong instruction in a
  $19.99 paid guide is a refund — treat its accuracy bar as higher than the app's own docs.
  A manual bundle that isn't pushed to the Bilko repo is not shipped; say so plainly.
- **Never guess a version bump from unconventional commit messages.** If the commit list
  doesn't cleanly map to `fix:`/`feat:`/`BREAKING CHANGE:` prefixes, `builder:classify-and-bump`
  asks the user which bump to apply rather than inferring one.

## Why nested skills instead of one inline sequence

Each step is its own file so it shows up as its own invocation in whatever surface tracks
skill/tool calls, and so a step can be changed (a different gate command, a new registry
target) without touching the others — same rationale as `pr-review-sweep` and
`issue-address`.

## What this skill is not

- Not a decision-maker on *whether* to release — it assumes the user (or an Epic) already
  wants the next diff shipped. If there's genuine ambiguity about scope, `builder:classify-and-bump`
  is the one step that pauses to ask.
- Not a registry-agnostic tool — `builder:publish` is npm-specific (see `buildTarget.cjs`'s
  `registry` field for future non-npm targets; out of scope for this version).
- Not wired to any UI button — invoking this skill is the only entry point today.

# builder:diff

Resolve what "already published" means for this project, then list every commit on `HEAD`
since that point.

## 1. Resolve the build target

Read `session-manager-operations/architecture/build-target.json` via
`resolveBuildTarget(cwd)` in `src/main/lib/buildTarget.cjs` (falls back to `package.json`'s
`name` if no explicit config exists). If `buildTarget.cjs` isn't present yet in this repo,
read `package.json`'s `name` field directly and note in the final report that the config
reader was missing — this does not block the pipeline.

## 2. Determine the last published point

Preferred: `npm view <packageName> version` — the actual registry state, not just a local
tag. This catches the case where a tag was pushed but the publish itself failed partway
(the tag would lie; the registry won't).

Fallback (no network, or `npm view` 404s because the package was never published): use the
last git tag instead — `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`.

## 3. Diff

```
git log <last-published-version-or-tag>..HEAD --oneline
```

If `npm view` returned a version not tagged locally, resolve its tag first (`git tag -l
'v<version>'`); if no matching local tag exists, fall back to comparing against
`git describe --tags --abbrev=0` and note the discrepancy in the report.

## Output

- The resolved package name and last-published version/tag (and which method resolved it —
  registry or git tag).
- The full commit list (subject lines) since that point.
- If the list is empty: stop here and report "nothing to publish" — do not proceed to
  `builder:classify-and-bump`.

# builder:classify-and-bump

Classify every commit subject from `builder:diff`'s output and pick the highest-severity
bump that applies.

## Rules (conventional commits)

- Any commit containing `BREAKING CHANGE:` in its body, or a `!:` right after the type/scope
  (e.g. `feat(api)!:`) → **major**.
- Any `feat:`/`feat(scope):` commit (and no breaking marker above) → **minor**.
- Any `fix:`/`fix(scope):` commit (and nothing higher) → **patch**.
- `chore:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `ci:` etc. with no `fix`/`feat`/breaking commit
  alongside them → **patch** (matches this project's own convention — see recent history,
  e.g. `chore(release): bump to v0.47.1` following a patch-only commit set).

Take the **highest** bump implied by the whole commit list (one `feat:` among ten `fix:`
commits still means minor; one breaking marker anywhere means major).

## When commits don't follow the convention

If a meaningful fraction of the commit list has no recognizable `type:` prefix at all (not
just an unconventional scope — genuinely no prefix, e.g. a bare "wip" or "updates"), **do
not guess**. Say so explicitly and ask the user which bump to apply, listing the
unclassifiable commits. This mirrors `pr-review-sweep:classify`'s needs-decision carve-out —
guessing wrong here ships an incorrect semver bump that's hard to walk back once published.

## Output

- The bump kind: `patch` | `minor` | `major`.
- The commit list grouped by which rule matched each one (for the eventual report step).
- If ambiguous: the question posed to the user instead of a bump kind, and the pipeline
  pauses here until answered.

# builder:publish

A dirty working tree in the main repo is **not** a blocker for this step — that's the whole
point of the isolated-worktree technique. Run the sequence below in order, without pausing
to ask for reconfirmation once `builder:gate` has passed.

## Procedure (exact order — verified across 4 real publishes)

1. **Bump the version, package.json only:**
   ```
   npm version <bump> --no-git-tag-version
   ```
   (`<bump>` is the kind decided by `builder:classify-and-bump` — `patch`/`minor`/`major`.)
   `--no-git-tag-version` matters: it updates `package.json`/`package-lock.json` without
   creating a git tag yet, so the tag step below can carry a proper message.

2. **Stage only the two version files — never `-A`:**
   ```
   git add package.json package-lock.json
   ```

3. **Commit, with a message listing the commits this release covers:**
   ```
   git commit -m "chore(release): bump to v<version>

   - <commit 1 subject>
   - <commit 2 subject>
   - ..."
   ```

4. **Tag the release commit:**
   ```
   git tag v<version>
   ```

5. **Create the isolated worktree from that tag:**
   ```
   git worktree add /tmp/sm-publish-v<version> v<version>
   ```

6. **Move into the worktree and build clean:**
   ```
   cd /tmp/sm-publish-v<version>
   npm ci
   npm run typecheck
   ```
   `npm ci` gives a fully clean `node_modules` from the lockfile — no leftover local state
   from the dirty main repo can leak into the published artifact.

7. **Publish from inside the worktree:**
   ```
   npm publish
   ```
   This project's `prepublishOnly` script runs `vite build` — because step 6 already `cd`'d
   into `/tmp/sm-publish-v<version>`, that build runs **inside the clean worktree**, never
   touching (or being affected by) the live/dirty working directory back in the main repo.
   This is the entire reason the worktree exists: it decouples "what's uncommitted in my
   editor right now" from "what gets built and shipped."

8. **Back in the main repo, push:**
   ```
   cd <main repo path>
   git push origin main
   git push origin v<version>
   ```

9. **Clean up the worktree:**
   ```
   git worktree remove /tmp/sm-publish-v<version> --force
   ```

10. **Verify the publish actually landed on the registry:**
    ```
    npm view <packageName> version
    npm view <packageName> dist-tags
    ```
    Confirm the reported version matches `<version>` and `latest` points to it (unless the
    project intentionally publishes to a different dist-tag).

## On any step failing

Stop at that step. Do not proceed. Report which step failed and its output. If the worktree
was already created (step 5+), leave it in place if its state is relevant evidence for
diagnosing the failure; otherwise remove it (step 9) before reporting, so a retry doesn't
collide with a stale `/tmp/sm-publish-v<version>` path.

## Output

- Version published.
- Confirmation the worktree was removed.
- `npm view` output proving the registry has the new version and correct dist-tag.
- Confirmation both `git push` calls succeeded (main + tag).

# builder:manual (step 5)

The manual is a **product we sell**, not documentation we generate. It has its own version
line, its own release cadence, and a buyer who paid $19.99 and is owed accuracy. This step
exists so a shipped feature never silently invalidates a paid chapter.

- **Source of truth:** `session-manager-operations/manual/` (see its `README.md` for the
  on-disk shape and the release checklist).
- **Build:** `npm run manual:build` → `~/Projects/Bilko/data/manual/releases/<version>/`.
- **Sold via:** the already-live `session_manager` Stripe SKU. There is no second price to
  create; entitlement already exists for every past buyer.

## Inputs

The commit list from `builder:diff` (step 0) and the version `builder:publish` (step 3) just
shipped. When run standalone, derive both the same way step 0 does.

## Procedure

### 1. Decide whether a revision is owed

Read `session-manager-operations/manual/manual.json`. Compare its `documentsAppVersion`
against the version just published.

Then map the release's commits onto the chapter list. A chapter is **affected** when a commit
in the diff touched a surface that chapter describes — check the chapter body for the file
paths, tab names, flags, and CLI invocations it names, and grep the diff for those.

Three outcomes, and only one of them is work:

| Finding | Action |
| --- | --- |
| No commit touches any documented surface | Bump `documentsAppVersion` only, note "no content change", stop. Do **not** cut a manual release for a version bump alone. |
| A commit changes behaviour a chapter describes | Revise that chapter. Continue to step 2. |
| A commit ships a surface no chapter covers | Report it as a **gap** — propose the new chapter, but do not author a whole chapter unprompted; that's a scope decision for the human or an Epic. |

### 2. Revise the affected chapters

Edit the chapter HTML in `session-manager-operations/manual/chapters/`.

Hard rules — these are the ones that protect a paying customer:

- **Every claim must be checkable against real code right now.** Read the file, run the
  command, confirm the constant. A wrong instruction in a paid product is a refund.
- **Never invent a screenshot.** A figure slot that has no captured image stays a
  `manual-figure__frame` placeholder stating what still needs capturing. Placeholder text is
  honest; a fabricated UI is not.
- **Don't restate the codebase.** The manual is an operator's guide — what a surface is for,
  the one thing people get wrong, the workflow that pays off. If a paragraph would be equally
  at home in `CLAUDE.md`, cut it.
- **Preserve the free chapter.** At least one chapter must stay `free: true` — it is the
  marketing sample, and `scripts/build-manual.mjs` refuses to build without one.

### 3. Bump the manual's own version

In `manual.json`:

- `documentsAppVersion` → the app version just published, always.
- `version` → **patch** for corrections and figure fills, **minor** for a revised or added
  chapter, **major** for a restructure that changes the chapter map. This is independent of
  the app's version — a buyer tracks the manual's line, not the app's.
- `releasedAt` → today, in the user's local timezone (America/Los_Angeles).

### 4. Build and verify

```bash
npm run manual:check     # sources valid, nothing written
npm run manual:build     # emits into ../Bilko/data/manual/releases/<version>/
```

The build is the gate. It refuses on a missing chapter file, a malformed or duplicated slug,
an asset declared without a source, or no free chapter. A refusal is a stop, not a warning.

Then confirm the bundle is real — the manifest must not over-promise:

```bash
ls ~/Projects/Bilko/data/manual/releases/<version>/
cd ~/Projects/Bilko && npx vitest run tests/manual.test.ts
```

That test walks the shipped manifest and asserts every chapter and asset it advertises
actually exists on disk.

### 5. Commit both repos

The bundle is served from the Bilko repo on Render, so an uncommitted bundle is an
unpublished manual. Two commits, one logical release:

- `session-manager`: the chapter sources + `manual.json`.
- `~/Projects/Bilko`: `data/manual/releases/<version>/`.

Per the project's standing rule, commit locally as soon as the build and test pass — don't
wait to be asked. Pushing the Bilko side is what actually ships it to buyers, so treat that
push with the same release trigger the npm publish gets.

## Output

Report, in this order:

1. Manual version before → after, and `documentsAppVersion` before → after.
2. Chapters revised, one line each, saying what changed and why.
3. Coverage gaps found (shipped surfaces with no chapter) — as proposals, not as work done.
4. Figures still pending capture, by chapter.
5. Whether the Bilko-side bundle is committed and pushed. If it isn't pushed, say plainly
   that buyers are still seeing the previous edition.

## What this step is not

- Not a screenshot pipeline. Capturing and annotating real app screenshots is its own PRD;
  until it lands, figures are placed by hand and unplaced slots render as honest placeholders.
- Not a marketing-copy editor. The sales page (`SessionManagerPage.tsx` in the Bilko repo) is
  separate from the product it sells.
- Not a pricing or entitlement change. The $19.99 `session_manager` SKU and the
  `MANUAL_PRODUCT_KEY` mapping in `shared/manual-catalog.ts` are deliberately fixed — changing
  either strands existing buyers and needs an explicit decision, not a release step.

{"parentUuid":"e8c17fda-5f77-4de3-8233-cedc6de551a2","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"2812133f-eee1-40df-a75b-2d6636ff18fe","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01Dk2hmu1nweGEVhNLVPSjDM","type":"tool_result","content":"1	<h1>Epics & Sessions — Terminal and Chat are one session</h1>
2	
3	<p class="lede">An Epic <em>is</em> a tagged Claude session. Not a folder of sessions, not a wrapper
4	around one — a 1:1 relationship. Once that clicks, the two views over it stop being confusing.</p>
5	
6	<h2>One session, two views</h2>
7	
8	<p>Every Epic mints exactly one <code>claudeSessionId</code> when it is created. Both ways of
9	talking to it attach to that same id:</p>
10	
11	<table class="manual-table">
12	  <thead><tr><th>View</th><th>What runs underneath</th><th>Best for</th></tr></thead>
13	  <tbody>
14	    <tr>
15	      <td><strong>Terminal</strong></td>
16	      <td>An interactive PTY: <code>claude --resume <sessionId></code> in the Epic's cwd.</td>
17	      <td>Anything needing approvals, interruptions, or you watching closely.</td>
18	    </tr>
19	    <tr>
20	      <td><strong>Chat</strong></td>
21	      <td>Headless: <code>claude -p --resume <sessionId></code>, streamed back as a feed.</td>
22	      <td>Long unattended turns, and reading back what happened.</td>
23	    </tr>
24	  </tbody>
25	</table>
26	
27	<p class="manual-note"><strong>Switching views hands the session over — it never forks it.</strong>
28	Attachment is mutually exclusive: exactly one view holds the session at a time. Context continuity
29	across the switch is the whole point, so if you ever see a fresh empty session after switching,
30	that's a bug worth reporting, not expected behaviour.</p>
31	
32	<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="epic-views">
33	  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Epic detail with the Terminal/Chat view toggle visible"></div>
34	  <figcaption>
35	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">1</span> The view toggle — one session, two renderings.
36	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">2</span> The verbosity dial (1 loudest → 5 quietest).
37	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">3</span> The Epic's event chain: prompt → PRD → response.
38	  </figcaption>
39	</figure>
40	
41	<h2>Creating an Epic: two independent choices</h2>
42	
43	<p>The New Epic card asks two separate questions, and it is worth being deliberate about both:</p>
44	
45	<ol class="manual-steps">
46	  <li><strong>Agent — who is working.</strong> A persona from your Agent Library
47	  (<code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code>). This also decides which model the session launches with:
48	  the persona's own <code>model:</code> field wins, falling back to your global default.</li>
49	  <li><strong>Mission — how they work.</strong> One of <em>feature</em>, <em>bug</em>, or
50	  <em>discussion</em>. This sets the grounding template the session opens with, and how eagerly
51	  the agent should decompose work into scheduled PRDs.</li>
52	</ol>
53	
54	<p>Those two, plus a one-line summary of what's actually grounding the session, compose the
55	opening prompt in a fixed order — <strong>Actor, Input, Mission</strong>, then your own goal text.
56	That's the AIM framework, and it's why an Epic tends to start productively instead of spending
57	three turns establishing context.</p>
58	
59	<h3>The "advanced" flip: the grounding board</h3>
60	
61	<p>Flip the New Epic card and you get an inventory of what this session will really load —
62	the CLAUDE.md files, skills, MCP servers, and hooks it will discover on disk, plus your git branch
63	and the other Epics in the project. It is an <strong>inspector, not a control panel</strong>: there
64	is no toggle to make the CLI skip a file it would otherwise find. Read it to understand why an
65	agent behaved a certain way.</p>
66	
67	<h2>Lifecycle: three states, one transition you care about</h2>
68	
69	<pre><code>proposed ──(Approve & start, or submitting the first prompt)──▶ active ──▶ completed</code></pre>
70	
71	<ul>
72	  <li><strong>proposed</strong> — reserved but not started. <em>Nothing has been spent yet.</em>

<p class="lede">An Epic <em>is</em> a tagged Claude session. Not a folder of sessions, not a wrapper
around one — a 1:1 relationship. Once that clicks, the two views over it stop being confusing.</p>

<h2>One session, two views</h2>

<p>Every Epic mints exactly one <code>claudeSessionId</code> when it is created. Both ways of
talking to it attach to that same id:</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>View</th><th>What runs underneath</th><th>Best for</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Terminal</strong></td>
      <td>An interactive PTY: <code>claude --resume <sessionId></code> in the Epic's cwd.</td>
      <td>Anything needing approvals, interruptions, or you watching closely.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Chat</strong></td>
      <td>Headless: <code>claude -p --resume <sessionId></code>, streamed back as a feed.</td>
      <td>Long unattended turns, and reading back what happened.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>Switching views hands the session over — it never forks it.</strong>
Attachment is mutually exclusive: exactly one view holds the session at a time. Context continuity
across the switch is the whole point, so if you ever see a fresh empty session after switching,
that's a bug worth reporting, not expected behaviour.</p>

<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="epic-views">
  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Epic detail with the Terminal/Chat view toggle visible"></div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">1</span> The view toggle — one session, two renderings.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">2</span> The verbosity dial (1 loudest → 5 quietest).
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">3</span> The Epic's event chain: prompt → PRD → response.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>Creating an Epic: two independent choices</h2>

<p>The New Epic card asks two separate questions, and it is worth being deliberate about both:</p>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>Agent — who is working.</strong> A persona from your Agent Library
  (<code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code>). This also decides which model the session launches with:
  the persona's own <code>model:</code> field wins, falling back to your global default.</li>
  <li><strong>Mission — how they work.</strong> One of <em>feature</em>, <em>bug</em>, or
  <em>discussion</em>. This sets the grounding template the session opens with, and how eagerly
  the agent should decompose work into scheduled PRDs.</li>
</ol>

<p>Those two, plus a one-line summary of what's actually grounding the session, compose the
opening prompt in a fixed order — <strong>Actor, Input, Mission</strong>, then your own goal text.
That's the AIM framework, and it's why an Epic tends to start productively instead of spending
three turns establishing context.</p>

<h3>The "advanced" flip: the grounding board</h3>

<p>Flip the New Epic card and you get an inventory of what this session will really load —
the CLAUDE.md files, skills, MCP servers, and hooks it will discover on disk, plus your git branch
and the other Epics in the project. It is an <strong>inspector, not a control panel</strong>: there
is no toggle to make the CLI skip a file it would otherwise find. Read it to understand why an
agent behaved a certain way.</p>

<h2>Lifecycle: three states, one transition you care about</h2>

<pre><code>proposed ──(Approve & start, or submitting the first prompt)──▶ active ──▶ completed</code></pre>

<ul>
  <li><strong>proposed</strong> — reserved but not started. <em>Nothing has been spent yet.</em>
  Every Epic is born here.</li>
  <li><strong>active</strong> — the session is running, authoring PRDs, receiving scheduler updates.</li>
  <li><strong>completed</strong> — archived to its own JSON file. The session id is dead; resuming
  mints a new one that traces back.</li>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>Don't repurpose an Epic.</strong> Its title and objective are fixed
for the life of its session — that objective <em>is</em> the first prompt. Iterate in follow-up
messages; when the unit of work changes, start a new Epic. The rename action in the row menu is for
fixing a typo, not for changing what an Epic is about.</p>

<h2>Where per-task behaviour belongs (and where it doesn't)</h2>

<p>This is the most common architectural mistake users make. Settings — including Permissions,
Hooks, MCP Servers — edits <em>on-disk files that the CLI reads on every single invocation</em>.

project. It is not per-conversation curation and never was.</p>

<p>The Chat feed has a five-level density dial, numbered loudest-first: <strong>1 raw</strong>,

<h2>The fields, in the order you'll fill them</h2>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>name</strong> — the filename on disk (<code>~/.claude/agents/<name>.md</code>).
  Must be lowercase and hyphenated (<code>^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$</code>); the app rejects anything else
  before it ever hits disk.</li>
  <li><strong>description</strong> — shown in the persona list and in every Agent picker. This is
  the line that gets folded into an Epic's opening prompt, so write it as a sentence about what
  this persona does, not a label.</li>
  <li><strong>default model</strong> — one of <code>inherit</code> / <code>haiku</code> /
  <code>sonnet</code> / <code>opus</code>. Leave it <code>inherit</code> only if you genuinely
  want this persona to ride whatever the launching view's own default is; otherwise pin it.</li>
  <li><strong>tools</strong> — a checklist of the tools this persona is granted
  (<code>Read</code>, <code>Grep</code>, <code>Glob</code>, <code>Bash</code>, <code>Write</code>,
  <code>Edit</code>, <code>WebFetch</code>, <code>WebSearch</code>, <code>Task</code>). Anything not
  ticked is refused at call time by the CLI, not by session-manager.</li>
  <li><strong>color</strong> — cosmetic only; shows as a swatch dot in the persona list.</li>
  <li><strong>tags</strong> — which Tag Library missions this persona is associated with. Purely a
  many-to-many bookkeeping field (see below), not a restriction on which Mission an Epic can pair
  it with.</li>
  <li><strong>definition</strong> — the system prompt body this persona runs under.</li>

<h2>Model resolution: how <code>--model</code> actually gets picked</h2>

<p>Both launch paths — <code>chatRunner.cjs</code>'s headless Chat run and
<code>EpicTerminalPane.tsx</code>'s interactive Terminal — resolve the same way, mirrored so the
two views of one Epic session never disagree on which model they're running:</p>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li>Look up the Epic's <code>agentType</code> (the persona it was created with).</li>
  <li>Read that persona's own <code>model</code> frontmatter field from
  <code>~/.claude/agents/<agentType>.md</code>.</li>

  <li>Otherwise fall back — Chat falls back to the hardcoded <code>sonnet</code> floor; Terminal

silently rather than throwing. The lookup never blocks a launch; the worst case is you get the
fallback model instead of the one you thought you set.</p>

<h2>Tags: the same relationship, editable from two pages</h2>

<p>A persona's <code>tags</code> field records which of Tag Library's missions it's associated
with. This is a genuine many-to-many relationship with one source of truth: assigning a tag from
this page's chip row and assigning an agent from Tag Library's own detail pane both write through
the identical <code>savePersona</code> call, to the identical frontmatter line. There is no second
copy to drift.</p>

<p>Claude Code itself resolves a project-local agent file

project shadowing it, and the detail pane's "project overrides" field lists them with a one-click

  <p>You open a persona, tighten its tool grants or rewrite its definition, save — and the next

<p class="lede">An Session <em>is</em> a tagged Claude session. Not a folder of sessions, not a wrapper
around one — a 1:1 relationship. Once that clicks, the two views over it stop being confusing.</p>

<h2>One session, two views</h2>

<p>Every Session mints exactly one <code>claudeSessionId</code> when it is created. Both ways of
talking to it attach to that same id:</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>View</th><th>What runs underneath</th><th>Best for</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Terminal</strong></td>
      <td>An interactive PTY: <code>claude --resume <sessionId></code> in the Session's cwd.</td>
      <td>Anything needing approvals, interruptions, or you watching closely.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Chat</strong></td>
      <td>Headless: <code>claude -p --resume <sessionId></code>, streamed back as a feed.</td>
      <td>Long unattended turns, and reading back what happened.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>Switching views hands the session over — it never forks it.</strong>
Attachment is mutually exclusive: exactly one view holds the session at a time. Context continuity
across the switch is the whole point, so if you ever see a fresh empty session after switching,
that's a bug worth reporting, not expected behaviour.</p>

<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="epic-views">
  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Session detail with the Terminal/Chat view toggle visible"></div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">1</span> The view toggle — one session, two renderings.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">2</span> The verbosity dial (1 loudest → 5 quietest).
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">3</span> The Session's event chain: prompt → PRD → response.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>Creating an Session: two independent choices</h2>

<p>The New Session card asks two separate questions, and it is worth being deliberate about both:</p>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>Agent — who is working.</strong> A persona from your Agent Library
  (<code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code>). This also decides which model the session launches with:
  the persona's own <code>model:</code> field wins, falling back to your global default.</li>
  <li><strong>Mission — how they work.</strong> One of <em>feature</em>, <em>bug</em>, or
  <em>discussion</em>. This sets the grounding template the session opens with, and how eagerly
  the agent should decompose work into scheduled PRDs.</li>
</ol>

<p>Those two, plus a one-line summary of what's actually grounding the session, compose the
opening prompt in a fixed order — <strong>Actor, Input, Mission</strong>, then your own goal text.
That's the AIM framework, and it's why an Session tends to start productively instead of spending
three turns establishing context.</p>

<h3>The "advanced" flip: the grounding board</h3>

<p>Flip the New Session card and you get an inventory of what this session will really load —
the CLAUDE.md files, skills, MCP servers, and hooks it will discover on disk, plus your git branch
and the other Sessions in the project. It is an <strong>inspector, not a control panel</strong>: there
is no toggle to make the CLI skip a file it would otherwise find. Read it to understand why an
agent behaved a certain way.</p>

<h2>Lifecycle: three states, one transition you care about</h2>

<pre><code>proposed ──(Approve & start, or submitting the first prompt)──▶ active ──▶ completed</code></pre>

<ul>
  <li><strong>proposed</strong> — reserved but not started. <em>Nothing has been spent yet.</em>
  Every Session is born here.</li>
  <li><strong>active</strong> — the session is running, authoring PRDs, receiving scheduler updates.</li>
  <li><strong>completed</strong> — archived to its own JSON file. The session id is dead; resuming
  mints a new one that traces back.</li>
</ul>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>Don't repurpose an Session.</strong> Its title and objective are fixed
for the life of its session — that objective <em>is</em> the first prompt. Iterate in follow-up
messages; when the unit of work changes, start a new Session. The rename action in the row menu is for
fixing a typo, not for changing what an Session is about.</p>

<h2>Where per-task behaviour belongs (and where it doesn't)</h2>

<p>This is the most common architectural mistake users make. Settings — including Permissions,
Hooks, MCP Servers — edits <em>on-disk files that the CLI reads on every single invocation</em>.
A Project-scope Settings change alters the substrate for every current and future Session in that

60	
61	<p>Flip the New Session card and you get an inventory of what this session will really load —

    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">3</span> The Session's event chain: prompt → PRD → response.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>Creating a Session: two independent choices</h2>

<p>The New Session card asks two separate questions, and it is worth being deliberate about both:</p>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>Agent — who is working.</strong> A persona from your Agent Library
  (<code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code>). This also decides which model the session launches with:
  the persona's own <code>model:</code> field wins, falling back to your global default.</li>
  <li><strong>Mission — how they work.</strong> One of <em>feature</em>, <em>bug</em>, or
  <em>discussion</em>. This sets the grounding template the session opens with, and how eagerly
  the agent should decompose work into scheduled PRDs.</li>
</ol>

<p>Those two, plus a one-line summary of what's actually grounding the session, compose the
opening prompt in a fixed order — <strong>Actor, Input, Mission</strong>, then your own goal text.
That's the AIM framework, and it's why a Session tends to start productively instead of spending
three turns establishing context.</p>

<h3>The "advanced" flip: the grounding board</h3>

<p>Flip the New Session card and you get an inventory of what this session will really load —
the CLAUDE.md files, skills, MCP servers, and hooks it will discover on disk, plus your git branch
and the other Sessions in the project. It is an <strong>inspector, not a control panel</strong>: there
is no toggle to make the CLI skip a file it would otherwise find. Read it to understand why an
agent behaved a certain way.</p>

<h2>Lifecycle: three states, one transition you care about</h2>

<pre><code>proposed ──(Approve & start, or submitting the first prompt)──▶ active ──▶ completed</code></pre>

<ul>
  <li><strong>proposed</strong> — reserved but not started. <em>Nothing has been spent yet.</em>
  Every Session is born here.</li>
  <li><strong>active</strong> — the session is running, authoring PRDs, receiving scheduler updates.</li>
  <li><strong>completed</strong> — archived to its own JSON file. The session id is dead; resuming
  mints a new one that traces back.</li>
</ul>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>Don't repurpose a Session.</strong> Its title and objective are fixed
for the life of its session — that objective <em>is</em> the first prompt. Iterate in follow-up
messages; when the unit of work changes, start a new Session. The rename action in the row menu is for
fixing a typo, not for changing what a Session is about.</p>

<h2>Where per-task behaviour belongs (and where it doesn't)</h2>

<p>This is the most common architectural mistake users make. Settings — including Permissions,
Hooks, MCP Servers — edits <em>on-disk files that the CLI reads on every single invocation</em>.
A Project-scope Settings change alters the substrate for every current and future Session in that
project. It is not per-conversation curation and never was.</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>You want…</th><th>Correct lever</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>This kind of task to behave differently</td><td>A custom <strong>Mission tag</strong> (its prompt template)</td></tr>
    <tr><td>A different reviewer/implementer style or model</td><td>A custom <strong>Agent persona</strong></td></tr>
    <tr><td>Different permissions, hooks, env vars, MCP servers</td><td><strong>Settings</strong> — genuinely substrate</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h2>Reading a session without drowning</h2>

<p>The Chat feed has a five-level density dial, numbered loudest-first: <strong>1 raw</strong>,
2 detail, 3 standard, 4 brief, <strong>5 summary</strong>. Tool cards appear only at levels 1–2.
Nothing is ever discarded from the store — raise the level and the byte-exact record comes back
with no re-read.</p>

<p>Two things ignore the dial on purpose, and you should know why:</p>

<ul>
  <li>A turn <strong>asking you something</strong> is never hidden or clamped at any level. Hiding
  a question strands a run waiting on an answer nobody can see.</li>
  <li>The <strong>in-flight</strong> bubble keeps its tool strip at every level — mid-run it's the
  only progress signal there is.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Project overrides — the mistake that costs the most time</h2>","originalFile":"<h1>Agent Library — authoring the "who" of a Session</h1>

<p class="lede">Agent Library is a full CRUD editor over <code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code> — the
same persona files the <code>claude</code> CLI already reads. It is not a viewer bolted onto the
filesystem; New, Duplicate, Save, Revert, and Delete all write straight through to disk, and every
persona you author here becomes a pickable <em>Agent</em> in the New Session card's "who is working"
column.</p>

<h2>What a persona actually controls</h2>

<p>A Session is always grounded by two independent choices: an <strong>Agent</strong> (this page —
the "who") and a <strong>Mission</strong> tag (Tag Library — the "what"). Picking a persona in the
New Session card does three concrete things, and only three:</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Where it lands</th><th>Notes</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><code>description</code></td>
      <td>Folded into the Session's opening prompt as an Actor framing line, before the grounding
      summary and the Mission template.</td>
      <td>Read once, at Session creation. Editing the persona afterward does not rewrite an existing
      Session's opening prompt.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>model</code></td>
      <td>Sets the <code>--model</code> the Session's session launches with, for <strong>both</strong>
      the Terminal view and the headless Chat view.</td>
      <td>Only fires when set to something other than <code>inherit</code>. Otherwise each view
      falls back to its own default (Chat: <code>sonnet</code>; Terminal: the raw-session-model
      toggle).</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><code>tools</code>, <code>color</code>, <code>tags</code>, definition body</td>
      <td>Written verbatim into the persona's frontmatter/body — read by the <code>claude</code>
      CLI or Tag Library, not re-interpreted by session-manager.</td>
      <td><code>tags</code> is a session-manager-only extension; the CLI itself never reads it.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="manual-note">Beyond those, <code>agentType</code> stays display-only. Picking a persona
does not change which <code>claude</code> binary spawns, and it does not swap out permissions,
hooks, or MCP servers — that substrate is Settings, not Agent Library. See the domain-model rule
in this manual's project reference: if you want a task to run under different settings, that's a
Settings edit; if you want it to run as a different <em>persona</em>, that's this page.</p>

<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="agent-library-editor">
  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Agent Library tab, a persona selected in the list, detail pane open showing model/tools/tags fields"></div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">1</span> The persona list — filterable, each row shows
    its color swatch and override count.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">2</span> <strong>default model</strong> — sets
    <code>--model</code> for this persona's Sessions.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">3</span> <strong>tags</strong> — the many-to-many link
    to Tag Library, editable from either side.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>The fields, in the order you'll fill them</h2>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>name</strong> — the filename on disk (<code>~/.claude/agents/<name>.md</code>).
  Must be lowercase and hyphenated (<code>^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$</code>); the app rejects anything else
  before it ever hits disk.</li>
  <li><strong>description</strong> — shown in the persona list and in every Agent picker. This is
  the line that gets folded into a Session's opening prompt, so write it as a sentence about what
  this persona does, not a label.</li>
  <li><strong>default model</strong> — one of <code>inherit</code> / <code>haiku</code> /
  <code>sonnet</code> / <code>opus</code>. Leave it <code>inherit</code> only if you genuinely
  want this persona to ride whatever the launching view's own default is; otherwise pin it.</li>
  <li><strong>tools</strong> — a checklist of the tools this persona is granted
  (<code>Read</code>, <code>Grep</code>, <code>Glob</code>, <code>Bash</code>, <code>Write</code>,
  <code>Edit</code>, <code>WebFetch</code>, <code>WebSearch</code>, <code>Task</code>). Anything not
  ticked is refused at call time by the CLI, not by session-manager.</li>
  <li><strong>color</strong> — cosmetic only; shows as a swatch dot in the persona list.</li>
  <li><strong>tags</strong> — which Tag Library missions this persona is associated with. Purely a
  many-to-many bookkeeping field (see below), not a restriction on which Mission a Session can pair
  it with.</li>
  <li><strong>definition</strong> — the system prompt body this persona runs under.</li>
</ol>

<h2>Model resolution: how <code>--model</code> actually gets picked</h2>

<p>Both launch paths — <code>chatRunner.cjs</code>'s headless Chat run and
<code>EpicTerminalPane.tsx</code>'s interactive Terminal — resolve the same way, mirrored so the
two views of one Session session never disagree on which model they're running:</p>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li>Look up the Session's <code>agentType</code> (the persona it was created with).</li>
  <li>Read that persona's own <code>model</code> frontmatter field from
  <code>~/.claude/agents/<agentType>.md</code>.</li>
  <li>If it's set and isn't <code>inherit</code>, use it.</li>
  <li>Otherwise fall back — Chat falls back to the hardcoded <code>sonnet</code> floor; Terminal
  falls back to its own raw-session-model toggle.</li>
</ol>

<p>Any failure in that chain — no matching Session, no persona file, an unreadable file — falls back
silently rather than throwing. The lookup never blocks a launch; the worst case is you get the
fallback model instead of the one you thought you set.</p>

<h2>Tags: the same relationship, editable from two pages</h2>

<p>A persona's <code>tags</code> field records which of Tag Library's missions it's associated
with. This is a genuine many-to-many relationship with one source of truth: assigning a tag from
this page's chip row and assigning an agent from Tag Library's own detail pane both write through
the identical <code>savePersona</code> call, to the identical frontmatter line. There is no second
copy to drift.</p>

<h2>Project overrides — the mistake that costs the most time</h2>

<p>Claude Code itself resolves a project-local agent file
(<code><project-cwd>/.claude/agents/<name>.md</code>) ahead of the global one at
<code>~/.claude/agents/<name>.md</code>, for any project that has one. Agent Library shows
you this directly: a persona row with an <strong>override</strong> badge names every currently-open
project shadowing it, and the detail pane's "project overrides" field lists them with a one-click
<strong>×</strong> to drop a project's local copy.</p>

<div class="manual-incident">
  <h3>Editing the global persona and wondering why nothing changed</h3>
  <p>You open a persona, tighten its tool grants or rewrite its definition, save — and the next
  Session launched from a specific project behaves exactly as before. The project has its own
  <code>.claude/agents/<name>.md</code> silently winning every time, and Agent Library's edit
  form never touches it — this page only creates and edits the <em>global</em> copy.</p>
  <p><strong>Rule:</strong> before editing a misbehaving persona, check the "project overrides"
  field for that name. If a project you're testing against is listed, either edit that project's
  local file directly or drop the override from here first.</p>
</div>

<p class="manual-note">Agent Library itself can only create the global definition — it has no
per-tab cwd context of its own, so there is no "create an override" button here. Overrides are
created by Claude Code's own file-discovery, or by hand; this page can only read and delete them.</p>

<h2>The workflow that pays off: focused personas instead of repeated instructions</h2>

<p>The failure mode this page exists to fix is retyping the same paragraph of constraints into
every prompt — "only read, never edit," "use opus for this, it needs judgement," "stick to these
three tools." Every one of those is a one-time persona edit instead of a recurring tax on your
attention:</p>

<ul>
  <li>A read-only research persona: tools trimmed to <code>Read</code>/<code>Grep</code>/<code>Glob</code>,
  model left cheap. Reuse it for every "just look and report" Session without re-explaining the
  constraint each time.</li>
  <li>A judgement-call persona: <code>model</code> pinned to <code>opus</code>, tagged against the
  Mission it's meant to pair with in Tag Library, so it surfaces as the suggested default there.</li>
  <li><strong>Duplicate</strong> an existing persona that's 90% right rather than authoring from
  scratch — it clones the full draft (name suffixed <code>-copy</code>) so you're editing, not
  retyping.</li>
</ul>

<p>The description field is the lever most people under-use: because it's folded into the Session's

Session rather than floating free. You will never need to hand-write a PRD file yourself.</p>","originalFile":"<h1>Scheduler — author once, run around your token window</h1>

<p class="lede">The Scheduler is the feature that pays for the app. You write a PRD, it lands in a
queue, and Session Manager runs it as a headless <code>claude -p</code> job timed around your plan's
rolling 5-hour token window — auto-pausing when you're rate-limited and resuming the moment the
window resets.</p>

<h2>What the Scheduler is a browser over</h2>

<p>It is a viewer and operator surface on one hierarchy, scoped to the active tab's project by
default ("All projects" is the explicit escape hatch):</p>

<pre><code>TAB (project)
└── EPIC (unit of work)
    └── PRD (one scheduled job)</code></pre>

<p>On disk, PRDs live at
<code><project>/session-manager-operations/scheduler/epics/<epic-id>/prds/</code>, with the
queue and history sharded alongside in <code>scheduler/state/</code>. Every PRD belongs to an Epic —
there is no such thing as a free-floating PRD.</p>

<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="scheduler-queue">
  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Scheduler tab, Queue view, at least one running job"></div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">1</span> Queue / PRDs / History — three views, one panel.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">2</span> Mode selector: manual · on-reset · when-available.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">3</span> A job's status badge — <em>needs_review</em> is a
    question, not a failure.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>The three run modes</h2>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>Mode</th><th>Behaviour</th><th>Use when</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td><code>manual</code></td><td>Nothing runs until you press go.</td><td>You're debugging the queue itself.</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>on-reset</code></td><td>Fires at each 5-hour window reset.</td><td>You want a predictable burst, not a trickle.</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>when-available</code></td><td>Polls your billing usage every 60 s and runs whenever there's headroom. <strong>The default.</strong></td><td>Almost always.</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h2>Concurrency: one pool, machine-wide</h2>

<p>Scheduler jobs and Chat runs draw from the <em>same</em> pool of concurrent <code>claude -p</code>
sessions (default 5, adjustable from the Home tab). On top of that sits a memory gate: a job won't
start if the machine doesn't have headroom for it. That gate is machine-aware rather than a
hardcoded job count, which is what makes running five parallel agents on a laptop survivable.</p>

<h2>Writing a PRD that actually finishes</h2>

<p>Two real incidents shaped every rule here, and both are worth internalising:</p>

<div class="manual-incident">
  <h3>The poll-hang</h3>
  <p>A PRD used <code>until $(curl … | jq .uptime)</code> to wait for a deploy. The condition was
  unsatisfiable — that deploy type never restarts the API — so the job spun for
  <strong>2 h 47 m</strong> until the watchdog killed it.</p>
  <p><strong>Rule:</strong> never write an unbounded wait. Every loop gets a maximum iteration
  count and an explicit give-up branch.</p>
</div>

<div class="manual-incident">
  <h3>The post-AC overrun</h3>
  <p>A PRD declared success, then launched a fixture generator over 50,000 seeds that appeared
  nowhere in its acceptance criteria. It ran <strong>2 h 44 m</strong> before a human killed it.</p>
  <p><strong>Rule:</strong> the acceptance criteria are the <em>ceiling</em>, not the floor. When
  the AC are met, stop.</p>
</div>

<h3>The checklist</h3>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li>One PRD, one outcome. If you can't state the outcome in a sentence, it's two PRDs.</li>
  <li>Acceptance criteria must be checkable <strong>headlessly</strong>. "Launch the app and click
  through the tabs" cannot be verified by a <code>claude -p</code> job — it has no GUI and will be
  SIGTERM'd.</li>
  <li>Every loop is bounded. Every wait has a timeout.</li>
  <li>Ordering comes from <code>dependsOn</code> — nothing else gates a batch.</li>
  <li>Never reuse a PRD number.</li>
</ol>

<h2>When a job parks in <code>needs_review</code></h2>

<p><code>needs_review</code> is <strong>a question, not a result</strong>. When a job lands there,
Session Manager writes a deterministic root-cause report next to that run's own log and appends it
as a response on the Epic that authored the PRD — so the question comes back to the conversation
that asked it, not to a global inbox you'll never check.</p>

<p>This is also the strongest argument for writing tight PRDs: the clearer the PRD, the less there
is to route back to you.</p>

<h2>Self-healing you don't have to think about</h2>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Boot reconciliation</strong> — on startup, jobs whose processes died are reaped and
  classified (success / timeout / error). A still-alive orphan is terminated gracefully first so its
  log isn't misread mid-write.</li>
  <li><strong>Dead-process reaper</strong> — periodic PID-liveness checks catch hung jobs.</li>
  <li><strong>Supervisor</strong> — every 15 minutes, a probe per running job; it kills a stuck
  poll-loop's shell without killing the agent that spawned it.</li>
  <li><strong>Definition-of-done gate</strong> — when the queue drains, completed PRDs are
  re-verified against their own acceptance criteria and a report is written. Idempotent, so a
  re-drain over the same set is a no-op.</li>
  <li><strong>External watchdog</strong> — an out-of-process timer relaunches the app if its
  heartbeat goes stale while jobs are outstanding.</li>
</ul>

<p class="manual-note">All of it exists so that "queue it and go to bed" is a real workflow rather
than an aspiration.</p>

async function main() {
  const outDir = join(outRoot, src.version);
  // Rebuild from scratch — a stale chapter left behind from a previous build of
  // the same version would ship silently.
  if (existsSync(outDir)) rmSync(outDir, { recursive: true });
  mkdirSync(outDir, { recursive: true });

  for (const c of chapterHtml) {
    writeFileSync(join(outDir, c.file), c.html, 'utf-8');
  }

  const figuresSrc = join(SOURCE, 'figures');
  if (existsSync(figuresSrc)) {
    cpSync(figuresSrc, join(outDir, 'figures'), { recursive: true });
  }

  const assets = [];
  for (const a of src.assets ?? []) {
    if (a.id === 'offline-html') {
      writeFileSync(join(outDir, a.file), offlineHtml, 'utf-8');
    } else if (a.id === 'pdf') {
      writeFileSync(join(outDir, a.file), await renderPdf(offlineHtml));
    } else if (existsSync(join(SOURCE, 'assets', a.file))) {
      cpSync(join(SOURCE, 'assets', a.file), join(outDir, a.file));

      // Declaring an asset the bundle doesn't contain hands buyers a broken
      // download button — refuse the build rather than ship it.
      fail(`asset "${a.id}" declares ${a.file} but no source exists at manual/assets/${a.file}`);
    }
    assets.push({
      id: a.id,
      label: a.label,
      file: a.file,
      mime: a.mime ?? 'application/octet-stream',
      bytes: statSync(join(outDir, a.file)).size,
    });
  }

  const manifest = {
    version: src.version,
    releasedAt: src.releasedAt,
    title: src.title,
    summary: src.summary,
    documentsAppVersion: src.documentsAppVersion,
    chapters: src.chapters.map(c => ({

      ...(c.free ? { free: true } : {}),
      file: c.file,
      ...(c.figures ? { figures: c.figures } : {}),

<p class="lede">Session Manager is a local cockpit for the Claude Code CLI. It does not replace
<code>claude</code>; it wraps it — giving you a terminal, a scheduler that runs work while you sleep,
and roughly two dozen configuration and observability surfaces over the same
<code>~/.claude/</code> directory the CLI already reads.</p>

<h2>1. Install and launch</h2>

<p>There is nothing to build. The app ships on npm and runs straight from <code>npx</code>:</p>

<pre><code>npx claude-code-session-manager@latest</code></pre>

<p>First launch recompiles the native terminal backend (<code>node-pty</code>) for your Electron
runtime, so give it a minute. Linux and macOS only.</p>

<p>If you want the stripped-down version — one terminal, no tabs, no config surface — add
<code>--simple</code>:</p>

<pre><code>npx claude-code-session-manager@latest --simple</code></pre>

  </figcaption>

<h2>2. The one idea to internalise: TAB = project, EPIC = unit of work</h2>

<p>Almost every mistake new users make comes from missing this. Session Manager has exactly two
levels of scope, and they are not interchangeable:</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>Concept</th><th>What it actually is</th><th>How many</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>TAB</strong></td>

      <td>One per project. Picking an already-open project re-activates its tab; it never opens a second.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>EPIC</strong></td>
      <td>One small unit of work inside that project, backed by its own tagged Claude session.</td>
      <td>Many per tab. Short-lived by design — one Epic per thing you're doing.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>The rule that follows:</strong> if you want a second conversation in
the same project, you want a second <em>Epic</em>, not a second tab. Tabs are for switching projects.</p>

<h2>3. Where your data lives</h2>

<p>When a tab first opens on a directory, Session Manager creates one folder inside it:</p>

<pre><code><your-project>/session-manager-operations/
├── prompt-sessions/   # your Epics — active index + archived Epics
├── scheduler/         # PRDs, queue, and run state
├── project-brief/     # the Home tab's project brief
└── logs/</code></pre>

<p>It is plain JSON and Markdown, it sits inside your repo, and it is meant to be read by humans and
committed if you want it committed. Nothing about your project is stored in a cloud service by this
app — the marketing page's "local-first" claim is literal.</p>

<h2>4. Your first five minutes</h2>

  <li>Press <strong>New Epic</strong>. Pick an <em>Agent</em> (who works) and a <em>Mission</em>
  (feature / bug / discussion), type what you want, and submit.</li>
  <li>Watch it run. That's the loop. Everything else in this manual is about doing that loop

</ol>

Pick an <em>Agent</em> (who works) and a <em>Mission</em>","originalFile":"<h1>Getting Started — the 10-minute setup</h1>

<p class="lede">Session Manager is a local cockpit for the Claude Code CLI. It does not replace
<code>claude</code>; it wraps it — giving you a terminal, a scheduler that runs work while you sleep,
and roughly two dozen configuration and observability surfaces over the same
<code>~/.claude/</code> directory the CLI already reads.</p>

<h2>1. Install and launch</h2>

<p>There is nothing to build. The app ships on npm and runs straight from <code>npx</code>:</p>

<pre><code>npx claude-code-session-manager@latest</code></pre>

<p>First launch recompiles the native terminal backend (<code>node-pty</code>) for your Electron
runtime, so give it a minute. Linux and macOS only.</p>

<p>If you want the stripped-down version — one terminal, no tabs, no config surface — add
<code>--simple</code>:</p>

<pre><code>npx claude-code-session-manager@latest --simple</code></pre>

<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="first-launch">
  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="app boot, Home tab, empty project list"></div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">1</span> The left nav — every surface lives here.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">2</span> <strong>Open / Start Project</strong> — the only
    way a project enters the app.
    <span class="callout" data-arrow="down">3</span> The Almanac footer: connection dot, 5-hour usage,
    active branch, app version.
  </figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>2. The one idea to internalise: TAB = project, SESSION = unit of work</h2>

<p>Almost every mistake new users make comes from missing this. Session Manager has exactly two
levels of scope, and they are not interchangeable:</p>

<table class="manual-table">
  <thead><tr><th>Concept</th><th>What it actually is</th><th>How many</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>TAB</strong></td>
      <td>A working directory. The cwd <em>is</em> the project identity — everything the app stores
      for a project keys off that path.</td>
      <td>One per project. Picking an already-open project re-activates its tab; it never opens a second.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>SESSION</strong></td>
      <td>One small unit of work inside that project, backed by its own tagged Claude session.</td>
      <td>Many per tab. Short-lived by design — one Session per thing you're doing.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="manual-note"><strong>The rule that follows:</strong> if you want a second conversation in
the same project, you want a second <em>Session</em>, not a second tab. Tabs are for switching projects.</p>

<h2>3. Where your data lives</h2>

<p>When a tab first opens on a directory, Session Manager creates one folder inside it:</p>

<pre><code><your-project>/session-manager-operations/
├── prompt-sessions/   # your Sessions — active index + archived Sessions
├── scheduler/         # PRDs, queue, and run state
├── project-brief/     # the Home tab's project brief
└── logs/</code></pre>

<p>It is plain JSON and Markdown, it sits inside your repo, and it is meant to be read by humans and
committed if you want it committed. Nothing about your project is stored in a cloud service by this
app — the marketing page's "local-first" claim is literal.</p>

<h2>4. Your first five minutes</h2>

<ol class="manual-steps">
  <li><strong>Open / Start Project</strong> in the left nav, and pick a repo you actually work in.
  A native folder picker opens; "New Folder" starts a fresh one.</li>
  <li>The Terminal tab boots a real <code>claude</code> session in that directory. This is the same
  CLI you already use — same settings, same skills, same MCP servers.</li>
  <li>Press <strong>New Epic</strong>. Pick an <em>Agent</em> (who works) and a <em>Mission</em>
  (feature / bug / discussion), type what you want, and submit.</li>
  <li>Watch it run. That's the loop. Everything else in this manual is about doing that loop
  faster, cheaper, and unattended.</li>
</ol>

<h2>5. What to read next</h2>

<p>If you only read two more chapters, read <a href="#epics-and-sessions">Epics & Sessions</a>
(so you stop losing context) and <a href="#scheduler">Scheduler</a> (so the app starts working
while you don't).</p>
