{"parentUuid":"cc79a74b-d750-4c87-9548-26c202c5eb3d","isSidechain":false,"attachment":{"type":"edited_text_file","filename":"/home/bilko/Projects/session-manager/session-manager-operations/manual/chapters/scheduler.html","snippet":"1	<h1>Scheduler — author once, run around your token window</h1>
2	
3	<p class="lede">The Scheduler is the feature that pays for the app. You write a PRD, it lands in a
4	queue, and Session Manager runs it as a headless <code>claude -p</code> job timed around your plan's
5	rolling 5-hour token window — auto-pausing when you're rate-limited and resuming the moment the
6	window resets.</p>
7	
8	<h2>What the Scheduler is a browser over</h2>
9	
10	<p>It is a viewer and operator surface on one hierarchy, scoped to the active tab's project by
11	default ("All projects" is the explicit escape hatch):</p>
12	
13	<pre><code>TAB (project)
14	└── SESSION (unit of work)
15	    └── PRD (one scheduled job)</code></pre>
16	
17	<p>On disk, PRDs live at
18	<code><project>/session-manager-operations/scheduler/epics/<epic-id>/prds/</code>, with the
19	queue and history sharded alongside in <code>scheduler/state/</code>. Every PRD belongs to a Session —
20	there is no such thing as a free-floating PRD.</p>
21	
22	<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="scheduler-queue">
23	  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Scheduler tab, Queue view, at least one running job"></div>
24	  <figcaption>
25	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">1</span> Queue / PRDs / History — three views, one panel.
26	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">2</span> Mode selector: manual · on-reset · when-available.
27	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">3</span> A job's status badge — <em>needs_review</em> is a
28	    question, not a failure.
29	  </figcaption>
30	</figure>
31	
32	<h2>The three run modes</h2>
33	
34	<table class="manual-table">
35	  <thead><tr><th>Mode</th><th>Behaviour</th><th>Use when</th></tr></thead>
36	  <tbody>
37	    <tr><td><code>manual</code></td><td>Nothing runs until you press go.</td><td>You're debugging the queue itself.</td></tr>
38	    <tr><td><code>on-reset</code></td><td>Fires at each 5-hour window reset.</td><td>You want a predictable burst, not a trickle.</td></tr>
39	    <tr><td><code>when-available</code></td><td>Polls your billing usage every 60 s and runs whenever there's headroom. <strong>The default.</strong></td><td>Almost always.</td></tr>
40	  </tbody>
41	</table>
42	
43	<h2>Concurrency: one pool, machine-wide</h2>
44	
45	<p>Scheduler jobs and Chat runs draw from the <em>same</em> pool of concurrent <code>claude -p</code>
46	sessions (default 5, adjustable from the Home tab). On top of that sits a memory gate: a job won't
47	start if the machine doesn't have headroom for it. That gate is machine-aware rather than a
48	hardcoded job count, which is what makes running five parallel agents on a laptop survivable.</p>
49	
50	<h2>Writing a PRD that actually finishes</h2>
51	
52	<p>Two real incidents shaped every rule here, and both are worth internalising:</p>
53	
54	<div class="manual-incident">
55	  <h3>The poll-hang</h3>
56	  <p>A PRD used <code>until $(curl … | jq .uptime)</code> to wait for a deploy. The condition was
57	  unsatisfiable — that deploy type never restarts the API — so the job spun for
58	  <strong>2 h 47 m</strong> until the watchdog killed it.</p>
59	  <p><strong>Rule:</strong> never write an unbounded wait. Every loop gets a maximum iteration
60	  count and an explicit give-up branch.</p>
61	</div>
62	
63	<div class="manual-incident">
64	  <h3>The post-AC overrun</h3>
65	  <p>A PRD declared success, then launched a fixture generator over 50,000 seeds that appeared
66	  nowhere in its acceptance criteria. It ran <strong>2 h 44 m</strong> before a human killed it.</p>
67	  <p><strong>Rule:</strong> the acceptance criteria are the <em>ceiling</em>, not the floor. When
68	  the AC are met, stop.</p>
69	</div>
70	
71	<h3>The checklist</h3>
72	
73	<ol class="manual-steps">
74	  <li>One PRD, one outcome. If you can't state the outcome in a sentence, it's two PRDs.</li>
75	  <li>Acceptance criteria must be checkable <strong>headlessly</strong>. "Launch the app and click
76	  through the tabs" cannot be verified by a <code>claude -p</code> job — it has no GUI and will be
77	  SIGTERM'd.</li>
78	  <li>Every loop is bounded. Every wait has a timeout.</li>
79	  <li>Ordering comes from <code>dependsOn</code> — nothing else gates a batch.</li>
80	  <li>Never reuse a PRD number.</li>
81	</ol>
82	
83	<p class="manual-note"><strong>PRD authoring is API-only.</strong> The <code>scheduler_create_prd</code>
84	MCP tool is the sole sanctioned way to write a PRD file — a hook blocks any other tool from writing
85	directly into a project's <code>scheduler/epics/<epic-id>/prds/</code> folder. It validates
86	frontmatter, atomically allocates the PRD number, and enforces that every PRD joins an existing
87	Session rather than floating free. You will never need to hand-write a PRD file yourself.</p>
88	
89	<h2>When a job parks in <code>needs_review</code></h2>
90	
91	<p><code>needs_review</code> is <strong>a question, not a result</strong>. When a job lands there,
92	Session Manager writes a deterministic root-cause report next to that run's own log and appends it
93	as a response on the Session that authored the PRD — so the question comes back to the conversation
94	that asked it, not to a global inbox you'll never check.</p>
95	
96	<p>This is also the strongest argument for writing tight PRDs: the clearer the PRD, the less there
97	is to route back to you.</p>
98	
99	<h2>Self-healing you don't have to think about</h2>
100	
101	<ul>
102	  <li><strong>Boot reconciliation</strong> — on startup, jobs whose processes died are reaped and
103	  classified (success / timeout / error). A still-alive orphan is terminated gracefully first so its
104	  log isn't misread mid-write.</li>
105	  <li><strong>Dead-process reaper</strong> — periodic PID-liveness checks catch hung jobs.</li>
106	  <li><strong>Supervisor</strong> — every 15 minutes, a probe per running job; it kills a stuck
107	  poll-loop's shell without killing the agent that spawned it.</li>
108	  <li><strong>Definition-of-done gate</strong> — when the queue drains, completed PRDs are
109	  re-verified against their own acceptance criteria and a report is written. Idempotent, so a
110	  re-drain over the same set is a no-op.</li>
111	  <li><strong>External watchdog</strong> — an out-of-process timer relaunches the app if its
112	  heartbeat goes stale while jobs are outstanding.</li>
113	</ul>
114	
115	<p class="manual-note">All of it exists so that "queue it and go to bed" is a real workflow rather
116	than an aspiration.</p>"},"type":"attachment","uuid":"c21b9a79-b2d5-472c-836c-0a78d21262f9","timestamp":"2026-08-08T05:56:21.121Z","userType":"external","entrypoint":"sdk-cli","cwd":"/home/bilko/Projects/session-manager/session-manager-operations/manual/chapters","sessionId":"59c63e2e-320e-41ea-a990-2f656feacb40","version":"2.1.220","gitBranch":"main"}

{"parentUuid":"f5eebbf7-7fd9-4574-a33c-f09be2cb1d8a","isSidechain":false,"attachment":{"type":"edited_text_file","filename":"/home/bilko/Projects/session-manager/session-manager-operations/manual/chapters/agent-library.html","snippet":"1	<h1>Agent Library — authoring the "who" of a Session</h1>
2	
3	<p class="lede">Agent Library is a full CRUD editor over <code>~/.claude/agents/*.md</code> — the
4	same persona files the <code>claude</code> CLI already reads. It is not a viewer bolted onto the
5	filesystem; New, Duplicate, Save, Revert, and Delete all write straight through to disk, and every
6	persona you author here becomes a pickable <em>Agent</em> in the New Session card's "who is working"
7	column.</p>
8	
9	<h2>What a persona actually controls</h2>
10	
11	<p>A Session is always grounded by two independent choices: an <strong>Agent</strong> (this page —
12	the "who") and a <strong>Mission</strong> tag (Tag Library — the "what"). Picking a persona in the
13	New Session card does three concrete things, and only three:</p>
14	
15	<table class="manual-table">
16	  <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Where it lands</th><th>Notes</th></tr></thead>
17	  <tbody>
18	    <tr>
19	      <td><code>description</code></td>
20	      <td>Folded into the Session's opening prompt as an Actor framing line, before the grounding
21	      summary and the Mission template.</td>
22	      <td>Read once, at Session creation. Editing the persona afterward does not rewrite an existing
23	      Session's opening prompt.</td>
24	    </tr>
25	    <tr>
26	      <td><code>model</code></td>
27	      <td>Sets the <code>--model</code> the Session launches with, for <strong>both</strong>
28	      the Terminal view and the headless Chat view.</td>
29	      <td>Only fires when set to something other than <code>inherit</code>. Otherwise each view
30	      falls back to its own default (Chat: <code>sonnet</code>; Terminal: the raw-session-model
31	      toggle).</td>
32	    </tr>
33	    <tr>
34	      <td><code>tools</code>, <code>color</code>, <code>tags</code>, definition body</td>
35	      <td>Written verbatim into the persona's frontmatter/body — read by the <code>claude</code>
36	      CLI or Tag Library, not re-interpreted by session-manager.</td>
37	      <td><code>tags</code> is a session-manager-only extension; the CLI itself never reads it.</td>
38	    </tr>
39	  </tbody>
40	</table>
41	
42	<p class="manual-note">Beyond those, <code>agentType</code> stays display-only. Picking a persona
43	does not change which <code>claude</code> binary spawns, and it does not swap out permissions,
44	hooks, or MCP servers — that substrate is Settings, not Agent Library. See the domain-model rule
45	in this manual's project reference: if you want a task to run under different settings, that's a
46	Settings edit; if you want it to run as a different <em>persona</em>, that's this page.</p>
47	
48	<figure class="manual-figure" data-figure="agent-library-editor">
49	  <div class="manual-figure__frame" data-capture="Agent Library tab, a persona selected in the list, detail pane open showing model/tools/tags fields"></div>
50	  <figcaption>
51	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="left">1</span> The persona list — filterable, each row shows
52	    its color swatch and override count.
53	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="up">2</span> <strong>default model</strong> — sets
54	    <code>--model</code> for this persona's Sessions.
55	    <span class="callout" data-arrow="right">3</span> <strong>tags</strong> — the many-to-many link
56	    to Tag Library, editable from either side.
57	  </figcaption>
58	</figure>
59	
60	<h2>The fields, in the order you'll fill them</h2>
61	
62	<ol class="manual-steps">
63	  <li><strong>name</strong> — the filename on disk (<code>~/.claude/agents/<name>.md</code>).
64	  Must be lowercase and hyphenated (<code>^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$</code>); the app rejects anything else
65	  before it ever hits disk.</li>
66	  <li><strong>description</strong> — shown in the persona list and in every Agent picker. This is
67	  the line that gets folded into a Session's opening prompt, so write it as a sentence about what
68	  this persona does, not a label.</li>
69	  <li><strong>default model</strong> — one of <code>inherit</code> / <code>haiku</code> /
70	  <code>sonnet</code> / <code>opus</code>. Leave it <code>inherit</code> only if you genuinely
71	  want this persona to ride whatever the launching view's own default is; otherwise pin it.</li>
72	  <li><strong>tools</strong> — a checklist of the tools this persona is granted
73	  (<code>Read</code>, <code>Grep</code>, <code>Glob</code>, <code>Bash</code>, <code>Write</code>,
74	  <code>Edit</code>, <code>WebFetch</code>, <code>WebSearch</code>, <code>Task</code>). Anything not
75	  ticked is refused at call time by the CLI, not by session-manager.</li>
76	  <li><strong>color</strong> — cosmetic only; shows as a swatch dot in the persona list.</li>
77	  <li><strong>tags</strong> — which Tag Library missions this persona is associated with. Purely a
78	  many-to-many bookkeeping field (see below), not a restriction on which Mission a Session can pair
79	  it with.</li>
80	  <li><strong>definition</strong> — the system prompt body this persona runs under.</li>
81	</ol>
82	
83	<h2>Model resolution: how <code>--model</code> actually gets picked</h2>
84	
85	<p>Both launch paths — <code>chatRunner.cjs</code>'s headless Chat run and
86	<code>EpicTerminalPane.tsx</code>'s interactive Terminal — resolve the same way, mirrored so the
87	two views of one Session never disagree on which model they're running:</p>
88	
89	<ol class="manual-steps">
90	  <li>Look up the Session's <code>agentType</code> (the persona it was created with).</li>
91	  <li>Read that persona's own <code>model</code> frontmatter field from
92	  <code>~/.claude/agents/<agentType>.md</code>.</li>
93	  <li>If it's set and isn't <code>inherit</code>, use it.</li>
94	  <li>Otherwise fall back — Chat falls back to the hardcoded <code>sonnet</code> floor; Terminal
95	  falls back to its own raw-session-model toggle.</li>
96	</ol>
97	
98	<p>Any failure in that chain — no matching Session, no persona file, an unreadable file — falls back
99	silently rather than throwing. The lookup never blocks a launch; the worst case is you get the
100	fallback model instead of the one you thought you set.</p>
101	
102	<h2>Tags: the same relationship, editable from two pages</h2>
103	
104	<p>A persona's <code>tags</code> field records which of Tag Library's missions it's associated
105	with. This is a genuine many-to-many relationship with one source of truth: assigning a tag from
106	this page's chip row and assigning an agent from Tag Library's own detail pane both write through
107	the identical <code>savePersona</code> call, to the identical frontmatter line. There is no second
108	copy to drift.</p>
109	
110	<h2>Turning a persona into an Action button</h2>
111	
112	<p>Any persona can carry a project scope, which promotes it to its own button in that project's
113	Sessions toolbar — a shortcut around the New Session card, never a second creation path. Three
114	frontmatter fields, all editable from this page's detail pane:</p>
115	
116	<table class="manual-table">
117	  <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>What it does</th></tr></thead>
118	  <tbody>
119	    <tr><td><code>projects</code></td><td>Which project cwds show this Action, or <code>*</code> for every project.</td></tr>
120	    <tr><td><code>action</code></td><td>The opening instruction — becomes the Session's goal, the way your own typed goal does from the New Session card.</td></tr>
121	    <tr><td><code>actionLabel</code></td><td>The button's text. Defaults to the persona name if left blank.</td></tr>
122	  </tbody>

# builder:report

Produce one concise summary of what happened, whether the pipeline reached publish or
stopped early.

## On a successful publish

Report:
- **Version**: previous → new (and bump kind: patch/minor/major).
- **Commits covered**: the full list from `builder:diff`, grouped by the classification
  `builder:classify-and-bump` assigned.
- **Gate result**: typecheck + test:unit, both PASS.
- **npm verification**: `npm view <packageName> version` and `dist-tags` output, confirming
  the registry matches.
- **Git state**: both `git push origin main` and `git push origin v<version>` confirmed;
  worktree removed.

## On an early stop (no diff, failed gate, ambiguous bump, or a publish-step failure)

Report exactly which step stopped the pipeline and why:
- `builder:diff` — "nothing to publish" (no commits since last release).
- `builder:classify-and-bump` — the question posed to the user, still unanswered.
- `builder:gate` — which command failed and its output.
- `builder:publish` — which numbered step failed, its output, and whether a worktree or
  local tag was left behind that a retry needs to account for.

## Output

One report, plain text, suitable for pasting into an Epic/PRD completion note or relaying
directly to the user — no separate file is written by this step.
